questions.title: Requiring certainty

questions.title: Missing requirements
questions.prompt: You must draft an easily revised proposal. You know its goal but lack some details.
options: Wait for every detail.
Draft with labeled assumptions and ask focused questions.
Invent missing facts and present them as confirmed.
Ask your manager to write it.
questions.reason: B makes honest progress. C misleads readers; A delays unnecessarily and D gives away your responsibility.

questions.title: Deadline versus privacy
questions.prompt: An unapproved personal tool would help you process private customer records faster.
options: Publish the records so others can help.
Ask the approved tool's support team for help.
Use approved systems, explain the deadline risk, and find an authorized alternative.
Request more time without explaining the obstacle.
questions.reason: C protects data while addressing delivery. A exposes it; B is useful but narrower, and D leaves people uninformed.

questions.title: A teammate is stuck
questions.prompt: A teammate may miss a milestone. Your own work has some flexibility.
options: Ask about the blocker, offer specific help, and coordinate deadlines.
Take over everything without asking.
Ignore the issue because it is not your assignment.
Offer time-management advice without understanding the blocker.
questions.reason: A supports the teammate and project. C leaves a known risk untouched; B oversteps and D assumes the cause.

questions.title: Competing deadlines
questions.prompt: Your manager adds an urgent task. You cannot finish it and your existing commitment on time.
options: Promise both despite knowing you cannot deliver.
Explain the conflict, agree priorities, and update affected people.
Ignore the new request until the original work is finished.
Ask which task matters more.
questions.reason: B makes a realistic plan. A knowingly creates false expectations; D starts the right conversation but omits follow-through.

questions.title: Evidence against your idea
questions.prompt: Tests suggest your design is less reliable. Approval is tomorrow.
options: Dismiss the tests because you have more experience.
Check the tests together and revise your recommendation if warranted.
Ask how the tests were run.
Hide the results until approval.
questions.reason: B checks evidence and acts on it. D conceals decision-relevant facts; A substitutes status for evidence and C is only a first step.

questions.title: An error in a sent report
questions.prompt: Your calculation error changes an important conclusion in a report already sent.
options: Correct only your own copy.
Notify readers promptly and send a clear correction.
Falsely blame the reviewer.
Quickly recheck the calculation before correcting it.
questions.reason: B protects readers from using the wrong result. C adds dishonesty; D is reasonable if verification is needed, but the error here is confirmed.

questions.title: Technical disagreement
questions.prompt: Two teammates disagree about implementation. No misconduct or immediate danger is involved.
options: Compare options against requirements and use the agreed decision process.
Escalate to senior leadership before discussing the reasoning.
Insult the other person's competence publicly.
Ask each person to explain benefits and risks.
questions.reason: A leads toward a decision. C attacks the person; B escalates prematurely and D is a useful part of A.

questions.title: Discriminatory remarks
questions.prompt: A coworker reports repeated discriminatory remarks and asks where to get help.
options: Tell them to tolerate it for team harmony.
Listen and explain reporting resources without promising secrecy you cannot guarantee.
Offer to locate reporting information.
Suggest personal support without explaining reporting options.
questions.reason: B supports appropriate handling. A discourages reporting; C helps but is narrower, while D does not fully address the concern.

questions.title: An expensive supplier gift
questions.prompt: A supplier offers an expensive gift while you evaluate its bid.
options: Ask for smaller gifts to make it easier to hide.
Decline and follow the relevant policy and reporting guidance.
Seek ethics guidance without accepting.
Ask a colleague where to find the policy.
questions.reason: B addresses the conflict directly. A deliberately evades oversight; C and D are reasonable ways to obtain guidance.

questions.title: A small gift with unclear rules
questions.prompt: A partner offers an inexpensive branded notebook. You do not know the gift rules.
options: Check policy and obtain any required approval before accepting.
Accuse the partner of bribery without checking.
Politely decline because you are uncertain.
Ask the partner to conceal it.
questions.reason: A resolves the uncertainty. D introduces concealment; C is defensible, while B makes an unsupported accusation.

questions.title: Restricted customer records
questions.prompt: A colleague without access asks you to bypass the slow access process.
options: Put the records on a public link.
Help request approved access and find a permitted alternative meanwhile.
Refuse without explaining the process.
Ask the data owner to arrange approved access.
questions.reason: B protects data and helps progress. A exposes it; D is useful but narrower, and C is unhelpful.

questions.title: Pressure to hide poor results
questions.prompt: A summary must represent overall performance, but someone asks you to omit unfavorable results.
options: Omit them to keep the person happy.
Report accurately, explain limitations, and describe improvement plans.
Alter the underlying data to erase the findings.
Discuss presenting the findings clearly without hiding them.
questions.reason: B combines honesty with next steps. C falsifies the record; A misleads and D can support B.

questions.title: A decision you disagreed with
questions.prompt: After discussion, the authorized owner chooses a reasonable, policy-compliant plan you did not prefer.
options: Help implement it and monitor results.
Secretly implement your own plan.
Repeat the same objection without new evidence.
Record the decision and reasoning, then proceed.
questions.reason: A supports a legitimate decision. B secretly overrides it; C stalls progress and D can usefully accompany A.

questions.title: Repeated missed handoffs
questions.prompt: A teammate keeps missing handoffs despite an earlier supportive conversation.
options: Cover silently forever.
Agree a recovery plan using specific impacts; involve the relevant lead as needed.
Humiliate them publicly.
Ask your lead for advice using factual examples.
questions.reason: B combines support and accountability. C harms trust; A hides the problem and D is a reasonable step toward resolution.

questions.title: A possible service outage
questions.prompt: You see signs of a serious live-service problem. You know the on-call contact but are not authorized to change the system.
options: Notify on-call immediately with your observations.
Make risky system changes yourself.
Wait for customer complaints.
Ask another teammate's opinion before reporting.
questions.reason: A gets qualified help promptly. B can worsen the incident; C and D delay an appropriate response.

questions.title: Evidence makes old work less useful
questions.prompt: Your team spent weeks on a feature. New evidence shows it will not solve the intended user problem.
options: Hide the evidence.
Review it, identify reusable work, and propose a revised plan.
Continue only because so much time was spent.
Share the findings and request a project review.
questions.reason: B adapts while preserving useful work. A blocks informed decisions; C defends past effort and D is a useful first step.

questions.title: An interrupted specialist
questions.prompt: A specialist keeps being interrupted while trying to raise a relevant concern.
options: Make room for them to finish before deciding.
Dismiss the concern because they did not speak loudly enough.
Guess their concern and speak for them.
Request a written note before the decision.
questions.reason: A gets the information directly. B judges speaking style rather than substance; C risks misrepresentation and D is a fallback.

questions.title: A safe small experiment
questions.prompt: You may test an improvement on a copy of non-sensitive material. It affects nobody else's work and is easy to undo.
options: Run a small test, compare results, and share useful findings.
Wait for guaranteed success.
Force all teams to adopt it without permission.
Save the idea for later without a reason to delay.
questions.reason: A learns safely and promptly. C exceeds your authority; B prevents learning and D postpones it.

questions.title: Too much credit
questions.prompt: A leader credits you with designing a feature. Your teammate designed it; you implemented it.
options: Leave the misunderstanding uncorrected.
Explain your contribution and credit the teammate's design.
Also claim another person's testing work.
Say only that it was a team effort.
questions.reason: B gives accurate credit. C adds a false claim; A leaves one intact and D does not clearly correct it.

questions.title: An experiment fails
questions.prompt: An approved, small experiment does not produce the hoped-for improvement.
options: Report the result, explain learning, and recommend next steps.
Call it successful because people worked hard.
Replace the results with invented positive findings.
Record the result without considering lessons.
questions.reason: A turns failure into useful learning. C falsifies evidence; B confuses effort with results and D misses the learning.

questions.title: Setting a checkpoint

questions.title: A request to guess

options: Give a range, label assumptions, and explain what would narrow it.
Present an exact number as certain.
Ask which assumptions matter most before refining the range.
Say estimating is impossible and stop.
questions.reason: A gives useful, honest information. B implies unsupported precision; C can help and D avoids a feasible task.

questions.title: A missed handoff owner

Criticize both teams in a broad email.
Bring the relevant people together to agree an owner and next step.
questions.reason: D resolves the ownership gap. C assigns blame without solving it; A waits and B leaves expectations unclear.

questions.title: Unexpected test results
questions.prompt: A small test performs worse than expected, and the result may change next week's plan.
options: Remove the result from the report.
Check the test conditions, share the finding, and recommend next steps.
Repeat it indefinitely until a positive result appears.
Ask a specialist to review the setup.
questions.reason: B investigates and informs the decision. A conceals relevant evidence; C cherry-picks and D is useful but incomplete.

questions.title: A tool you have not used
questions.prompt: You need an unfamiliar approved tool for a task due in three days.
options: Pretend you already know it.
Wait until the deadline to ask for help.
Learn the essentials, test on sample material, and seek focused help early.
Ask for documentation without starting.
questions.reason: C combines learning and delivery. A misrepresents your ability; B delays help and D is only a starting point.

questions.title: A decision record is missing
questions.prompt: You join a project where people remember an important decision differently.
options: Check available evidence with the decision owner, then record the confirmed decision.
Write your preference as if it were the original decision.
Use the most senior person's recollection without checking.
Ask teammates what they remember.
questions.reason: A clarifies facts and prevents recurrence. B falsifies history; C assumes rank settles memory and D gathers partial evidence.

questions.title: Helping within limits
questions.prompt: A colleague asks for a full day of help, but you can spare one hour without missing your own deadline.
options: Agree to the full day and hide the impact.
Refuse without explaining.
Cancel your existing deadline without discussion.
Offer the hour, identify the main blocker, and discuss other help or priorities.
questions.reason: D is helpful and realistic. A conceals a known conflict; B is unhelpful and C changes commitments unilaterally.

questions.title: Recurring complaints
questions.prompt: Several users report a confusing form, but your internal dashboard shows few errors.
options: Tell users the dashboard proves there is no issue.
Review examples and user steps, then test whether the measure misses confusion.
Delete the complaints from the tracker.
Ask support for more details.
questions.reason: B checks both the experience and the metric. C destroys useful evidence; A dismisses it and D starts an investigation.

questions.title: A minor visual issue
questions.prompt: An accurate internal report is due now. Only optional spacing changes remain.
options: Delay indefinitely until the layout is perfect.
Claim the spacing is a critical defect to justify lateness.
Send the report on time and improve the template later.
Ask whether a brief delay is acceptable.
questions.reason: C distinguishes essential quality from polish. B misrepresents the issue; A overprioritizes it and D may add unnecessary delay.

questions.title: A major defect near release
questions.prompt: A required test finds a serious defect shortly before release.
options: Hide the failed test to preserve the date.
Ask a qualified colleague to verify the result promptly.
Remove the test without approval.
Inform the release owner, assess impact, and agree remediation or a release change.
questions.reason: D addresses the risk openly. A conceals known evidence; C bypasses the safeguard and B can support D.

questions.title: A better idea from a junior colleague
questions.prompt: A junior teammate proposes a simpler approach supported by credible evidence.
options: Compare it fairly and use it if it better meets the requirements.
Reject it because they are junior.
Claim you originated the idea.
Ask them to explain the evidence.
questions.reason: A evaluates substance and gives fair consideration. C steals credit; B relies on status and D is useful clarification.

questions.title: A slow approval
questions.prompt: You need approval for a consequential change. The approver is unavailable and the deadline is close.
options: Proceed and add their name as approval.
Seek the documented alternate approver and explain the schedule risk.
Prepare reversible work while waiting, without making the restricted change.
Wait silently and miss the deadline.
questions.reason: B pursues authorized action. A fabricates approval; C is sensible preparation and D hides the risk.

questions.title: A mistaken assumption
questions.prompt: You learn that an assumption in your plan is wrong, but no irreversible action has happened yet.
options: Keep using it to avoid admitting the mistake.
Change the plan privately without updating affected people.
Explain the change, revise the plan, and confirm any affected commitments.
Ask the source to confirm the new information.
questions.reason: C updates both the work and expectations. A knowingly relies on false information; B misses coordination and D is verification.

questions.title: A confidential example
questions.prompt: You want to use a previous client case in a presentation, but it contains restricted details.
options: Copy it into the slides because the audience is internal.
Use an approved anonymized or synthetic example and check the sharing rules.
Send the original to your personal email for editing.
Ask the information owner what may be shared.
questions.reason: B communicates the lesson within restrictions. C moves restricted material to an unapproved channel; A assumes internal means authorized.

questions.title: A weak project forecast
questions.prompt: New demand data suggests your project will deliver little benefit relative to its remaining cost.
options: Continue only because it is your project.
Hide the data until next quarter.
Ask the sponsor to review the data.
Present the evidence with options to stop, reduce, or redirect the work.
questions.reason: D enables a useful decision. B conceals relevant facts; A protects ownership over impact and C is a narrower first step.

questions.title: A harsh but useful review
questions.prompt: A reviewer is unnecessarily blunt, but identifies a real problem in your work.
options: Fix the valid issue and separately address the tone respectfully.
Ignore the issue because the tone was poor.
Retaliate with personal insults.
Ask for a concrete example of the problem.
questions.reason: A separates substance from delivery. C escalates personal conflict; B misses learning and D helps clarify.

questions.title: A colleague asks you to sign off
questions.prompt: Someone asks you to mark a mandatory review complete even though you have not performed it.
options: Sign because they are trustworthy.
Refuse the false sign-off and arrange the actual review or escalate the timing issue.
Backdate the sign-off to avoid scrutiny.
Ask how long a proper review would take.
questions.reason: B preserves an honest safeguard. C adds deliberate falsification; A also misrepresents completion and D is planning only.

questions.title: An unclear handoff message
questions.prompt: You receive a task with no deadline, owner contact, or acceptance criteria.
options: Invent all details and tell others they were agreed.
Ignore the task.
Clarify the essential expectations and propose a practical first step.
Ask for the deadline only.
questions.reason: C clarifies what matters without waiting for unnecessary detail. A fabricates agreement; B stalls and D leaves other key gaps.

questions.title: An improvement worth sharing
questions.prompt: A small approved change saves your team time, and another team has the same problem.
options: Force them to adopt it.
Keep it secret to preserve your advantage.
Offer to show the results if they ask.
Share the results and limitations, and offer help with a small trial.
questions.reason: D shares learning without imposing a solution. B withholds useful knowledge for personal advantage; A oversteps and C is passive.

sets.title: Working through tension
sets.subtitle: Stay clear when things get complicated.

questions.title: Checking your interpretation
questions.prompt: I check that I understood a disagreement before arguing against it.
questions.reason: Respond to the actual concern rather than an assumption about it.

questions.title: Avoiding difficult conversations
questions.prompt: I avoid mentioning a serious team problem because the conversation may be awkward.
questions.reason: Respectful early discussion is often better than allowing a serious problem to grow.

questions.title: Respectful challenge

questions.reason: Challenge the evidence and reasoning while preserving respect.

questions.title: Private criticism

questions.reason: Gossip damages trust and rarely establishes a fair solution.

questions.title: Assuming intent

questions.title: Giving specific feedback

questions.title: New evidence after a decision

questions.title: Respecting boundaries

questions.title: Fair recognition

questions.title: Unverified allegations

questions.title: Appropriate reporting

questions.reason: Serious concerns need appropriate handling, not informal pressure to stay quiet.

questions.title: Changing communication

questions.title: Concealing disagreement

questions.title: Knowing who decides

questions.title: Meeting inclusion

questions.title: Public embarrassment

questions.reason: Humiliation discourages learning and reporting problems.

questions.title: Acknowledging impact

questions.reason: Good intent does not remove the need to understand and repair harm.

questions.title: Team versus truth
questions.prompt: I hide a teammate's serious mistake to show loyalty.
questions.reason: Support the person while addressing the error; concealment can harm everyone affected.

options: I check that I understood another person.

I mentor people patiently.

questions.title: A heated meeting
questions.prompt: Two colleagues start talking over each other while deciding a routine design issue.
options: Choose the more confident speaker.
Interrupt to insult both of them.
Restate the shared goal, let each explain, and compare the options.
Suggest a short break, then return to the issue.
questions.reason: C restores a useful discussion. B adds personal hostility; A rewards confidence rather than evidence and D may help reset the tone.

questions.title: A missed reply
questions.prompt: A colleague has not replied to your important message. You do not know why.
options: Follow up clearly, state the deadline, and use an appropriate alternate channel if needed.
Tell the team they are deliberately obstructing you.
Wait silently until the deadline passes.
Check whether they are available.
questions.reason: A addresses the practical need without assuming intent. B makes an unsupported accusation; C stalls and D offers partial context.

questions.title: A correction in public
questions.prompt: You notice a factual error in a colleague's presentation that could mislead today's decision.
options: Stay silent to avoid awkwardness.
Mock the error in front of everyone.
Send a private note that may not be read until tomorrow.
Correct the point respectfully and offer to verify the detail together.
questions.reason: D protects the decision without humiliation. B attacks the person; A leaves misinformation and C may be too late.

questions.title: An upset colleague
questions.prompt: A colleague looks distressed as you leave. You can spare five minutes but have a firm commitment afterward.
options: Promise to stay all night although you cannot.
Check in, listen if they want, and be honest about your available time.
Ignore them solely because emotions do not belong at work.
Offer a specific later time to talk if they would prefer.
questions.reason: B offers genuine support within real limits. A makes a knowingly false promise; C dismisses the person and D can supplement B.

questions.title: Conflicting specialist advice
questions.prompt: Two qualified specialists recommend different options. You own a reversible decision due today.
options: Wait indefinitely for them to agree.
Pretend both approved your preferred option.
Compare assumptions and risks, decide within your authority, and set a review point.
Ask each specialist for their key concern.
questions.reason: C uses expertise without requiring endless consensus. B fabricates approval; A stalls and D is useful input.

questions.title: A decision has new risk
questions.prompt: After an agreed plan begins, you find credible new evidence of a serious risk.
options: Raise the evidence promptly with the owner and propose how to assess it.
Stay silent because the decision is final.
Invent additional problems to make your concern more persuasive.
Record the risk for a later review only.
questions.reason: A permits informed adaptation. C falsifies the case; B suppresses evidence and D may be too late for a serious risk.

questions.title: A complaint about your tone
questions.prompt: A teammate says your comments felt dismissive. You intended to be efficient.
options: Explain that intent is all that matters.
Ask for examples, acknowledge the impact, and agree how to communicate better.
Tell others the teammate is too sensitive.
Take time to reflect before responding respectfully.
questions.reason: B turns feedback into improvement. C spreads a personal judgment; A dismisses impact and D is useful preparation.

questions.title: Remote teammates excluded
questions.prompt: Important decisions repeatedly happen at a time when a relevant remote teammate cannot attend.
options: Keep the pattern because the majority prefers it.
Record decisions but refuse questions afterward.
Tell the teammate to stop complaining.
Arrange accessible input, share context, and adjust scheduling where practical.
questions.reason: D makes needed expertise available. C dismisses a real coordination issue; A and B preserve exclusion.

questions.title: Unfair credit in a summary
questions.prompt: A project summary omits a colleague who made a major contribution. You are reviewing it before publication.
options: Suggest a factual correction with the contribution included.
Add yourself as the sole contributor.
Say nothing because it is not your recognition.
Ask the author how contributions were collected.
questions.reason: A corrects the record directly. B introduces a false claim; C leaves the omission and D can clarify the cause.

questions.title: A rumor about misconduct
questions.prompt: You hear an unverified claim about misconduct and have no direct evidence.
options: Repeat it publicly as confirmed.
Use an appropriate reporting channel, clearly distinguishing what you heard from what you observed.
Investigate by accessing restricted personal records without permission.
Ask the reporting resource how to raise a secondhand concern.
questions.reason: B allows appropriate handling without claiming certainty. C violates access boundaries; A spreads an unverified accusation and D is reasonable guidance-seeking.

questions.title: A favored colleague breaks a rule
questions.prompt: You witness a friend bypassing an important control that applies to everyone.
options: Ignore it because they are your friend.
Delete the evidence to protect them.
Address or report the concern through the appropriate process using factual observations.
Ask the control owner how the rule applies.
questions.reason: C treats the issue fairly. B deliberately conceals it; A applies favoritism and D may clarify but should not erase a known concern.

questions.title: A disagreement blocks handoff
questions.prompt: A routine disagreement has resisted direct discussion and now blocks another team's deadline.
options: Summarize options and impacts, then involve the designated decision owner.
Secretly sabotage the other proposal.
Continue the same debate with no decision date.
Ask the affected team to explain its deadline needs.
questions.reason: A escalates appropriately after direct attempts failed. B is sabotage; C prolongs the block and D adds useful context.

questions.title: Unclear feedback
questions.prompt: Your manager says your update was confusing but gives no examples.
options: Ignore the feedback as useless.
Ask which parts were unclear and propose a shorter structure to test.
Claim everyone else understood without checking.
Review the update for jargon yourself.
questions.reason: B seeks actionable clarification and tries an improvement. C invents support; A dismisses learning and D can help but may miss the actual issue.

questions.title: A customer is angry
questions.prompt: A customer complains sharply about a real delay. You cannot fix it immediately.
options: Promise an immediate fix you know is impossible.
Argue about their tone instead of the delay.
Acknowledge the impact, explain what is known, and commit to a realistic next update.
Ask for details needed to route the issue.
questions.reason: C combines empathy with an honest commitment. A knowingly misleads; B ignores the problem and D can support triage.

questions.title: You disagree with the majority
questions.prompt: Most teammates favor an option, but you have specific evidence of an overlooked cost.
options: State the evidence respectfully and suggest comparing it against the shared goal.
Say nothing because disagreement is disloyal.
Invent a safety concern so people listen.
Ask whether the cost was already considered.
questions.reason: A adds relevant evidence constructively. C fabricates risk; B withholds input and D is a useful clarification.

questions.title: A quiet new hire
questions.prompt: A new hire rarely speaks in planning meetings, and you need their relevant analysis.
options: Assume they have nothing to add.
Offer context and a clear opportunity to share their analysis, without forcing a performance.
Ridicule their silence to encourage confidence.
Invite them to send comments before the meeting.
questions.reason: B makes participation accessible. C humiliates; A assumes lack of value and D is a useful alternative channel.

questions.title: A colleague needs instruction
questions.prompt: A colleague asks a basic question about a process you know well.
options: Give the answer and point to a clear reference if helpful.
Tell them publicly they should already know.
Send an unexplained technical document.
Ask which step is confusing before explaining.
questions.reason: A helps efficiently with a reusable reference. B discourages questions; C may not resolve confusion and D is useful clarification.

questions.title: Team loyalty and an error
questions.prompt: A teammate asks you not to disclose their important error because it may embarrass them.
options: Agree and let others rely on the incorrect work.
Help them blame a third person.
Offer support in correcting and communicating the error promptly.
Explain privately why affected people need accurate information.
questions.reason: C supports the person without concealing the problem. B adds false blame; A risks harm and D supports the right conversation.

questions.title: Different communication styles

options: Agree a concise summary format and ask focused questions respectfully.
Call them incompetent in the team chat.
Stop reading all their messages.
Ask for the main recommendation first.
questions.reason: A improves the working pattern. B attacks the person; C loses information and D is a useful immediate request.

questions.title: After conflict is resolved

options: Keep criticizing the other person privately.
Tell others they were dishonest without evidence.
Avoid all future coordination.
Follow through on your actions and check that the handoff works.
questions.reason: D rebuilds trust through execution. B spreads a baseless accusation; A and C prolong conflict.

questions.title: Useful outcomes

questions.title: Honest forecasts

questions.title: Evidence quality

questions.title: Disclosing conflicts

questions.title: Knowing limits

questions.title: Reviewing impact

questions.title: Authority checks
